hints: Notice the wording observable interference fringes - the bright and dark positions must stay still long enough for the eye to see them.
Connect a fixed fringe pattern to a constant phase difference at each point, which needs the same wavelength and a stable phase relationship between the two light waves.
Compare coherence with polarisation and equal amplitudes in the options - the latter two change fringe sharpness but do not decide whether stable fringes exist.
walkthrough: Identify the situation: light from two sources overlaps in space, so the resultant displacement at each point is the superposition of the two waves.
State the rule for a stable pattern: constructive interference needs constant path-difference plus constant source phase difference, and destructive interference needs the same stability.
Explain coherence: coherent means same frequency and constant phase difference, so $\phi_2 - \phi_1 = \text{constant}$ and the positions of maxima and minima do not move randomly.

Check the other conditions: polarisation state affects which components can superpose and amplitude equality affects minimum intensity $I_{min}$, but neither is necessary for some stable intensity variation to exist.
Conclude that coherence is the necessary condition for observable, stationary fringes. This is option C.

options.A: Polarised light can interfere, but polarisation is not required for fringes to form.
options.B: Unpolarised light can still interfere if the overlapping components have the same plane of vibration.
options.C: Coherent waves have the same frequency and a constant phase difference, so the fringe positions stay fixed and observable.
options.D: Equal amplitudes give maximum fringe contrast but unequal amplitudes still give visible intensity variation.
